template.title: Preparation
template.subtitle: Get ready to build
template.intro: You have an idea and the first conclusions from your conversations. Now lay out what needs to be done for the first version, get help if you need it, and gather the files and things to start with. A person working alone can go through this stage without a team.
general.title: General
general.intro: This part applies to every startup. SaaS, Hardware, B2B and B2C add their own points only when the startup has that category.
general/rozmowy.title: Talk to the people you want to help
general/rozmowy.guide_body:
Now you'll check your earlier assumptions in conversations. You'll look for specific events showing whether the problem occurs, how it gets in the way and what people do about it. Prepare a place for notes and a few supporting questions.
Find at least five people to talk to
Go back to the recipient description from point 1. Look for people who do the task in question. For the shop example, invite someone responsible for ordering stock. Simply working in a shop may not be enough.
Start with friends, referrals, themed groups, local businesses or events. You can write: “I'm trying to understand how owners of small shops plan their stock orders. Could you spare 15 minutes to tell me how it works for you?”. The time given is an example of a short meeting proposal.
A friend is a suitable interviewee if they fit the group. It's worth reaching beyond your own circle too. Five conversations are the start this exercise expects. Don't treat this number as a guarantee that the needs of the whole group are already known.
Ask about events and listen to the answers
At the start, explain what topic you want to understand. Leave the description of the solution for later, so you don't hint to the interviewee what you want to hear. Helpful questions are:
What did the last restocking in your shop look like?
At what moment did the difficulty appear? What happened then?
How often does a similar situation happen?
What was done then to cope, and what was the result?
How much time did it take you or how much did it cost? Where does that estimate come from?
You don't have to read the questions out in order. Follow up on unclear answers: “What do you mean?” or “Can you give an example?”. If someone says the current way is good enough, let them explain. Avoid the question “Do you also waste time on those awful files?”, which suggests a judgment.
When an idea for a new feature comes up, ask in what situation it would be needed. This way you learn the reason for the request. If the interviewee wants to see your idea, first finish the part about experiences and clearly separate the later presentation.
Write down each conversation separately
In the note, include the date, a short description of the interviewee's role, the specific case, the frequency, the current way of doing things and the effects. Also write down situations in which the problem didn't occur or didn't matter much. Mark a quote as a quote only if you remember the exact words. Record only with the interviewee's consent.
Separate the answer from your own conclusion. “He said he compared files for an hour” is information from the conversation. “He'll want to pay to save time” is your assumption. If there's no answer, write “no information”.
Compare the conversations and improve the assumptions
Line up the answers against the same questions: who has the difficulty, how often, what they do about it and how much it bothers them. In a small group, writing “3 of 5 people described such a case” is clearer than a lone “60%”. Don't extend this result to all potential customers.
List the recurring observations and, separately, what contradicts the idea. If only some interviewees experience the problem, check what they have in common. It may be worth narrowing the group. If the accounts are unclear or contradictory, write down the specific unknown and choose further conversations to clarify it.
After this point you have notes from the conversations, shared observations and an improved problem description. Also go back to point 2 if the proposed solution no longer fits what came out of the conversations.
general/rozmowy.guide_sources.0: Eric Migicovsky, How to Talk to Users. Basis: conversations about specific experiences, current ways of doing things and difficulties. The link leads to a summary and a recording of the lecture.
general/rozmowy.guide_sources.1: Paul Graham, Do Things that Don't Scale. Basis: reaching the first recipients personally.
general/rozmowy.guide_sources.2: Paul Graham, Before the Startup. Basis: building knowledge about users.
general/rozmowy/znajdz-rozmowcow.title: Find people to talk to
general/rozmowy/znajdz-rozmowcow/osoby.q: Find at least 5 people the chosen problem may affect.
general/rozmowy/znajdz-rozmowcow/osoby.h: Enter a name or a description, so you know whom the conversation was with. They don't have to be strangers — start with acquaintances from the industry.
Don't present your idea at the start. Ask about what they did, not what they would do.
general/rozmowy/zapytaj-o-doswiadczenia/: After each conversation, write down what you learned from it.
When did this problem last come up and how often does it happen? How does this person deal with it? What's most bothersome about it, and how much time, money or effort does it cost them?
Recordings or notes from the conversations
general/rozmowy/podsumuj-rozmowy.title: Sum up the conversations
general/rozmowy/podsumuj-rozmowy/powtarz: What came up repeatedly in the answers?
Something three people out of five said matters more than the most interesting remark of one.
general/rozmowy/podsumuj-rozmowy/za-i-pr: What suggests this problem is worth solving, and what undermines your assumptions?
Also write down what you didn't like. Contradicting evidence is worth more than ten confirmations.
general/scope.title: What can we do ourselves? And what not?
general/scope.guide_body:
Lay out the tasks to be done
Go back to the idea from the Idea Stage and list the work needed to prepare the first simple version someone can use. Choose the tasks that lead to the main benefit for the user. You can consider extras later.
Write down specific work results. “Prepare a sign-up form” lets you judge who can do it. The general heading “technology” says little about the help needed.
For each task, mark whether you can do it, need to learn something or are looking for someone to do it. Example entries: prepare user instructions — I'll do it myself; launch a simple form — I'll learn to use the chosen tool; make an enclosure model — I need someone who can design it.
For learning, choose skills tied to a specific task. “I'll learn to make a form” helps you find the right instructions. “I'll learn to program” covers much more work. If gaining a skill would push the start back a lot, consider help from someone else.
§
Do you need a co-founder
A co-founder is a person with whom you build the company together and share responsibility for its future. Look for one when you need a long-term contribution in an important area. The size of a single task alone doesn't decide whether you need a partner.
In the profile, describe what this person is to be responsible for. Example: “Preparing the first version of the program and developing it further after the tests”. Then match the requirements: what similar work they should already be able to show, what kind of cooperation you expect and how much time they can regularly commit.
Equity is a share of ownership of the company. Treat the range you enter as an initial proposal for discussion. Take into account responsibility and the contribution to further development. Doing a single task alone doesn't give grounds for setting a percentage. Discussing the split early is advisable, but there's no “task for a percentage” conversion rate.
If help with a specific piece of work is enough, move on to the people needed for a specific task.
§
People needed for a specific piece of work
Use the tasks that need help but have a defined end. It may be preparing graphics, making a model, a technical consultation or checking a specific solution.
Describe the skill that will let this task be done. Example: “I need a packaging design ready to send to the printer. I'm looking for someone who has prepared such files before”.
Give the amount you can spend on this work. If you have no budget, mark that. When looking for help, it's clear right away what terms you can offer.
general/scope.guide_sources.0: Michael Seibel, How to Plan an MVP (Startup School, 2019): limiting the first version to the basic benefit.
general/scope.guide_sources.1: Michael Seibel, One Order of Operations for Starting a Startup (2018): the skills needed for the first solution.
general/scope.guide_sources.2: Y Combinator, 10 Questions to Discuss with a Potential Co-founder (2023): responsibility, time, expectations and equity.
general/scope/tasks.title: Lay out the tasks for the first version
general/scope/tasks/mvp_tasks.question: A list of things that have to be done for the first version.
general/scope/tasks/mvp_tasks.help: Choose the tasks that lead to the main benefit. You can add extras later.
general/scope/tasks/mvp_tasks.example:
Prepare user instructions.
Launch a simple form.
Make an enclosure model.
general/scope/split.title: Split these tasks
general/scope/split/alone.question: Which of these things can you do on your own?
general/scope/split/alone.help: If there are no such tasks, write “none”.
general/scope/split/learn.question: Which ones can you learn?
general/scope/split/learn.help: Choose a skill tied to a specific task. If learning would push the start back a lot, move the task to help from others.
general/scope/split/learn.example: Launch a simple form in the chosen tool.
general/scope/split/others.question: Which ones do you need other people for?
general/scope/split/others.help: If you can manage on your own, write “none”.
general/scope/mode.title: Are you looking for people?
general/scope/mode/choice.question: How do you want to go through this stage?
general/scope/mode/choice.help: Choosing “I can manage on my own” skips looking for people, the joint trial and the rules of cooperation. The files and the list of gaps remain.
general/scope/mode/choice.config.options: I can manage on my own
I'm looking for contractors, not a co-founder
I'm looking for a co-founder and contractors
general/scope/cofounder.title: Co-founder profile
general/scope/cofounder/profile.question: Describe whom you're looking for as a co-founder.
general/scope/cofounder/profile.help: One item is one role. You can add your own field if something is missing from the profile.
general/scope/cofounder/profile.example: Responsibility: the first version of the program and its development after the tests. Equity: 15–25% for discussion.
general/scope/cofounder/profile.config.c: What this person is responsible for
What they should be able to show
What kind of cooperation you expect
How much time they can commit
general/scope/helpers.title: People needed for a specific piece of work
general/scope/helpers/roles.question: Tasks that are too small for a co-founder, but that you won't do on your own.
general/scope/helpers/roles.help: For each item, write the skill and whether you can pay for this work.
general/scope/helpers/roles.example: A packaging design ready for the printer. I'm looking for someone who has prepared such files. Budget: $200.
general/scope/helpers/roles.config.colum: Can you pay, and how much
general/find-help.title: Get help and the first contacts
general/find-help.guide_body:
Profile and invitation
Use the information from point 1 to complete the profile of yourself and the project. A person viewing the profile should quickly understand what you're building, what stage you're at and what they can help with. If you already have a suitable description, reuse it.
Show what you bring yourself: knowledge of the problem, access to recipients, a finished sketch or a skill needed for building. Add whether you're looking for a co-founder, someone for a specific task or a short consultation.
Example: “I'm building a holder for carrying shopping by bike. I have a sketch and conclusions from conversations with cyclists. I'm looking for someone to help prepare a model of the mount”.
If you're already working with suitable people, invite them to the project. Looking for more makes sense when a specific need remains.
§
Whom to ask
Choose people whose skills fit the tasks you've written down. Look at an example of similar work or ask for a short description of what the person has done before. You can search in Vairo, among friends or through referrals.
Write briefly what you need and what terms you can offer. Example: “I'm looking for help with a model of a bike holder. I saw your mount design. Can I show you the sketch and ask about working together?”.
After the reply, fill in the table row. Something specific is enough: “She replied, she has made models of similar parts, we agreed on a joint trial”. When someone hasn't replied yet, leave the contact as pending.
Compare the fit to the task, availability and the agreed terms. Add to the cooperation the people who have confirmed they want to take part. In the next point you'll check how working together goes.
general/find-help.guide_sources.0: Michael Seibel, One Order of Operations for Starting a Startup (2018): building with people with complementary skills.
general/find-help/social.title: Use the Social layer
general/find-help/social/opened.question: Complete your own and the startup's profile, then look for people in the Vairo network.
general/find-help/social/opened.help: This step opens Social. Tick it when the profile is ready and you know whom you're looking for.
general/find-help/outreach.title: Write down whom you're asking for help
general/find-help/outreach/contacts.ques: Contacts: the person or company, whether they replied, what skills they have and whether you'll work together.
general/find-help/outreach/contacts.help: One item is one conversation. When someone hasn't written back yet, enter “waiting”.
general/find-help/outreach/contacts.exam: Ola Kowalska. She replied. She has made models of similar parts. We're arranging a joint trial.
general/find-help/pick.title: Choose people from the platform
general/find-help/pick/people.question: Tick the people you want to go further with.
general/find-help/pick/people.help: These are real profiles from Vairo. You send the invitation to the startup from the person's card in Social. Ticking alone doesn't create a membership. If you're not choosing anyone, save an empty list.
general/trial.title: Check whether you can work together
general/trial.guide_body:
A joint task
From point 1, choose a piece of work whose result will be useful in the project and that can be finished in a few days. It could be a sketch of one part, a simple form or preparing part of the service to show a recipient.
Before you start, agree on what should be ready, who will prepare which parts and when you'll put them together. Match the work to the skills of the people taking part.
Example: “Ola will prepare a model of the mount, and I'll provide the dimensions and check the fit with the basket. On Friday we'll look at the result together”.
After the task, write down the outcome. Example: “A model of the mount was made. It fits the chosen basket, but the hook needs fixing”. Such an entry also shows what can be used further.
§
What's next for this line-up
Discuss whether the agreed result was achieved and whether each person could do their part. If something got stuck, work out the cause: missing skills, time or the necessary information.
Confirm whether you want to continue. Write down only the change that needs to be made, for example: “We're continuing. Before the next model, I'll hand over the full set of dimensions first”. If everything fits, “We're continuing with this line-up” is enough.
Team readiness here means you have an agreed line-up and can take on further work. One successful trial gives the first information about cooperation. A harder task may bring up further issues.
general/trial.guide_sources.0: Y Combinator, 10 Questions to Discuss with a Potential Co-founder (2023): a joint trial project.
general/trial.guide_sources.1: Michael Seibel, The Scientific Method for Startups (2016): testing an assumption and drawing a conclusion from the result. Applying it to a cooperation trial is an adaptation.
general/trial/task.title: Choose a joint task
general/trial/task/which.question: Which small task from the list are you taking on as a trial?
general/trial/task/which.help: It should use different skills and take a few days at most.
general/trial/task/which.example: A model of the bike holder mount.
general/trial/task/plan.question: What should be created, who does which part and when do you finish?
general/trial/task/plan.help: One sentence per person is enough.
general/trial/task/plan.example: Ola will prepare the model, I'll provide the dimensions. On Friday we look at the result.
general/trial/result.title: Write down the result of the trial
general/trial/result/outcome.question: What was created and what can you use it for?
general/trial/result/outcome.help: A short description or a link. The result stays as an ordinary answer in this stage.
general/trial/result/outcome.example: A model of the mount was made. It fits the basket, but the hook needs fixing. Link: …
general/trial/result/decision.question: What's next for this line-up?
general/trial/result/decision.help: If you're not changing anything, “We're continuing with this line-up” is enough. Otherwise write down only the change needed.
general/trial/result/decision.example: We're continuing. Before the next model, I'll hand over the full set of dimensions first.
general/trial/result/ready.question: The team is ready for further work.
general/trial/result/ready.help: Tick it when you have an agreed line-up. One trial doesn't have to solve everything.
general/workspace.title: Set up a place to work
general/workspace.guide_body:
Gather the materials
In Files, gather the current materials needed going forward: the idea description, useful conclusions from conversations and the results of the tasks so far. Choose the documents you or the team will come back to.
Name them so it's clear what they contain. Examples: “Idea description”, “Conclusions from conversations”, “Mount model”. When you have several versions, mark the one you're currently working on.
Share the materials with the people who need them and check that they can open them. You can complete the sub-point when the documents are gathered and available to the people who will use them.
§
Rules of cooperation
Agree on availability, the way of keeping in touch, decision-making and the terms of participation. Use earlier agreements if they still apply.
Write down short, accepted rules. Examples: “Each of us spends about five hours a week on the project”. “We send information about tasks in the shared chat”. “We approve expenses together”. “Ola does the paid task described in the agreed offer”.
Choose the entries that fit your situation. If a matter remains unagreed, mark it as open. If you're working alone, skip this sub-point.
general/workspace.guide_sources.0: Y Combinator, 10 Questions to Discuss with a Potential Co-founder (2023): availability, expectations and the way of resolving disagreements.
general/workspace/files.title: Gather the materials in Files
general/workspace/files/collected.questi: Upload the project's current materials to the Files section and share them with the people who will use them.
general/workspace/files/collected.help: Tick it when the documents are in one place and can be opened.
general/workspace/rules.title: Agree on the rules of cooperation
general/workspace/rules/agreements.help: Availability, the way of keeping in touch, decision-making and the terms of participation. Mark an unagreed matter as open.
general/workspace/rules/agreements.examp:
Each of us spends about five hours a week on the project.
We approve expenses together.
general/supplies.title: Gather the things needed to start
general/supplies.guide_body:
What's missing to start
Look at the first tasks and check whether anything is missing to do them. Add only what you currently need. If you have everything that lets you start, don't add items just to fill the list.
For a missing thing, check how to get it. You can buy material, borrow equipment, use a workshop or use a tool someone on the team already has. Enter the specific source if you know it.
The point is to get things within the available budget. Free access or borrowing can limit start-up spending.
For the cost, an approximate amount is enough. Add whether you pay once, monthly or per use. Enter an unknown price as “to be checked”. Write “free” when it's already known there will be no fee.
Example: printing the first model of the mount. The university workshop, after access is agreed. About $15 for the material for one print, the amount to be confirmed.
general/supplies.guide_sources.0: Dominika Blackappl, Practical Design: MVP Spec (2016): fitting the first version to what can be made and the costs.
general/supplies.guide_sources.1: Michael Seibel, How to Plan an MVP (Startup School, 2019): simple means to start.
general/supplies/missing.title: What's missing to start?
general/supplies/missing/items.question: Add only the missing things.
general/supplies/missing/items.help: The name, where you'll get it and the approximate cost. An empty list means you can start with what you already have.
general/supplies/missing/items.example: Printing the first model. The university workshop. About $15 for the material.
general/supplies/missing/items.config.co: Name, you can add a link
I'll buy it, borrow it, the team has it
saas.title: SaaS
saas.intro: Add the access rules, the cost of the first tests and — if the first version is paid — what happens to the account after payment.
saas/access.title: Work out who has access to what
saas/access.guide_body:
Whose data it is
Imagine two different customers using the program. Work out which materials belong to each of them and whether they are to share anything.
In a program for private notes, each person can have their own materials. In a program for companies, employees can use their company's shared space. Each employee can still log in with their own account.
Example: “Each company has its own space with documents. Its employees use individual accounts. One company's documents are unavailable to the other companies”.
§
What each role can do
Work out what individual people can do. It's enough to state which materials they can see, change and delete and whether they can invite others.
Example: the owner of the space can see, change and delete the company's documents, and also invite employees and remove their access. A collaborator can see and change shared documents but doesn't manage other people's access.
Add only the types of users you need in the first version. If everyone uses only their own materials and everyone has the same capabilities, one entry is enough.
Go over the entry with the person building the program. You should be able to answer the question: “Can this person see or change this document?”. Building these rules into the program and checking the security will happen during the build.
saas/access.guide_sources.0: Microsoft, Tenancy models for a multitenant solution: dividing into customers, users and their data.
saas/access.guide_sources.1: Alex Kracov, The First 90 Days of Building a SaaS Startup: agreeing on how the product works with the people building it.
saas/access/space.title: Whose data it is
saas/access/space/model.question: Do users have separate data, or do they share a space, for example a company's or a team's?
saas/access/space/model.help: Write down the chosen approach in one specific sentence.
saas/access/space/model.example: Each company has its own documents. Employees log in with their own accounts. Company A can't see company B's documents.
saas/access/roles.title: What each role can do
saas/access/roles/permissions.question: Write down the permissions of each type of user.
saas/access/roles/permissions.help: One item is one role. If everyone can do the same things, one entry is enough.
saas/access/roles/permissions.example: The owner sees, changes and deletes the company's documents and invites people. A collaborator sees and changes shared documents but doesn't manage access.
saas/access/roles/permissions.config.col: E.g. the owner of the space
What they can change or delete
E.g. their own documents, not other people's
saas/test-cost.title: Check how much the first tests will cost
saas/test-cost.guide_body:
Calculate the cost of the tests
Start with the number of people you want to invite to the tests. Also estimate how much they'll use the program. At first this will be an approximation that you'll improve after the first tests.
The number of accounts alone may not be enough. In a program that processes recordings, their length matters. In a program that stores files, the space taken up also counts.
Example: “We're inviting 10 testers. Each will process about 5 hours of recordings a month. In total that's 50 hours, or 3,000 minutes of recordings”.
Use the amounts written down in the general part and check the missing prices. The earlier list may have covered only things to start with. Here you're interested in the costs of the services needed to run the program during the tests.
Separate the fixed fee from the usage fee. A fixed fee is a set amount per period, for example a month of hosting the program on a server. A usage fee depends on the amount used, for example minutes of recording or the amount of data. One service can have both kinds of fees.
An example with made-up amounts: a server at $15 a month, recording processing at $0.01 a minute. At 3,000 minutes, processing costs $30. In total about $45 a month.
Write down the amount and the assumptions it comes from. If you don't know something yet, mark it as “to be checked”. Don't enter an unknown cost as zero.
§
Limit and budget
Check what the provider will do when a limit is exceeded: charge extra, stop the service or require moving to a more expensive plan. Note whether the limit applies to the whole program or to a single user.
Compare the estimated cost with the amount you can spend on the tests. Include your own testing of the program and the possibility of more use than you initially assume.
If the cost is too high, limit what drives it up: the number of testers, the length of the recordings processed or the number of files stored.
Example: “To start, we're inviting 10 people. Each can process up to 5 hours of recordings a month. Once the limit is used up, further recordings wait until the next month”.
Agree with the person building the program on how such a limit will work. Writing it down in Vairo alone won't stop the provider from charging fees.
If an extra limit is unnecessary, a short justification is enough, for example: “The chosen plan has a fixed price and blocks file uploads once the available space is used up, with no automatic extra charges”.
saas/test-cost.guide_sources.0: Stripe, How to start a SaaS business: the costs of infrastructure and services.
saas/test-cost.guide_sources.1: Microsoft, Pricing models for a multitenant solution: linking costs to usage and the importance of limits.
saas/test-cost.guide_sources.2: Userpilot, How to build a product launch plan for SaaS: starting with a limited group and a small scope.
saas/test-cost/usage.title: How many testers and how much they'll use
saas/test-cost/usage/plan.question: How many testers will you invite and how much will each use?
saas/test-cost/usage/plan.help: Give the number of people and the unit that really generates the cost: time, space or the number of operations.
saas/test-cost/usage/plan.example: 10 people, each will process about 5 hours of recordings a month. 50 hours in total.
saas/test-cost/usage/monthly.question: What's the estimated monthly cost of the services for this group?
saas/test-cost/usage/monthly.help: Start from the prices on the list of gaps in General. Add the fixed fee and the usage fee. For an unknown price write “to be checked”, not zero.
saas/test-cost/usage/monthly.example: A server at $15 a month plus $0.01 per minute of recording. At 3,000 minutes it comes to about $45 a month.
saas/test-cost/limits.title: What happens after exceeding a limit
saas/test-cost/limits/overage.question: What will happen when the limits of the chosen services are exceeded?
saas/test-cost/limits/overage.help: For each service write: an extra charge, the service stopping or having to change plan. Mark whether the limit is for the whole program or per user.
saas/test-cost/limits/overage.example:
Once the space is used up, the provider blocks new files and doesn't charge extra.
Processing recordings beyond the plan costs more per minute.
saas/test-cost/limits/cap.question: What limit are you putting on the tests to stay within budget?
saas/test-cost/limits/cap.help: The number of testers, hours or space. If an extra limit is unnecessary, write briefly why.
saas/test-cost/limits/cap.example: 10 people, up to 5 hours of recordings a month per person. After the limit, further recordings wait until the next month.
saas/paid.title: Set the rules for paid access
saas/paid.guide_body:
How the customer pays and gets access
Use the billing method chosen in the Idea Stage. Work out how the first person will pay and what has to happen for them to be able to use the paid version.
With a simple offer, you can use a ready-made payment link. If you're serving only a few people at first, you can grant access by hand after checking the payment in the payment provider's dashboard.
Example: “The customer pays through a link assigned to the chosen offer. After confirming the payment in the provider's dashboard, we unlock their account and let them know they can start using it”.
With manual handling, agree on who checks the payments and how long the customer will wait for access. You also have to keep track of subsequent payments and the end of the paid period.
If access is to switch on automatically, the person building the program has to connect it to the information from the payment provider. A payment link alone doesn't mean the account will be unlocked automatically.
With a usage-based fee, also work out where you'll get the information about the amount used, for example the number of tasks done.
§
What happens in typical situations
Go through the situations in the task. For each one, write down what the user can do and from when their capabilities change.
Start with a successful payment. Work out when the customer gets access and for how long. If you offer a free trial, decide what happens after it ends: which capabilities remain and what the user has to do to keep using it. If there's no such trial, write “Not applicable”.
With a failed payment, distinguish the first purchase from a renewal. A person who is only just creating an account is in a different situation from a customer who has been using the program for several months and suddenly has a problem with their card. Decide whether an existing customer gets extra time and when use will be restricted.
Consider cancelling the renewal separately. Write down until when the customer can use the capabilities already paid for and when further charges stop. Then work out what happens after the paid period ends. Include the possibility of viewing and downloading saved materials.
Example: “After cancelling the renewal, the customer uses it until the end of the paid period. Afterwards they can view and download saved documents but can't add new ones or edit existing ones”.
Match the rules to your offer. Ending paid access, deleting the account and deleting saved materials are separate decisions.
Finally, check with the person building the program that the chosen way of handling payments lets you apply your agreements. The same rules should be clearly presented to the customer.
saas/paid.guide_sources.0: Stripe, Create subscriptions: handling subscriptions with ready-made tools and payment links.
saas/paid.guide_sources.1: Stripe, Using webhooks with subscriptions: payment information and access management.
saas/paid.guide_sources.2: Stripe, Cancel subscriptions: cancelling renewal and ending after the paid period.
saas/paid/choice.title: Is the first version paid?
saas/paid/choice/answer.question: Will anyone pay for access in the first version?
saas/paid/choice/answer.help: If not, the rest of this point drops out. You'll come back to it when you change the answer.
saas/paid/choice/answer.config.options.n: No, the first version is free
saas/paid/how.title: How the customer pays and gets access
saas/paid/how/flow.question: How will the customer pay and how will they get access?
saas/paid/how/flow.help: Write who checks the payment and whether the account is switched on by hand or automatically.
saas/paid/how/flow.example: The customer pays through the offer link. After the payment shows up in the provider's dashboard, we unlock the account by hand and write to say they can start.
saas/paid/cases.title: When access starts and ends
saas/paid/cases/paid_ok.question: The customer has paid for access. From when can they use it and for how long?
saas/paid/cases/paid_ok.help: One sentence. With a usage fee, add where you get the usage information.
saas/paid/cases/paid_ok.example: Access switches on the same day and lasts until the end of the paid month.
saas/paid/cases/trial.question: The free trial has ended. What remains, and what requires payment?
saas/paid/cases/trial.help: If there's no free trial, write “Not applicable”.
saas/paid/cases/trial.example: After 14 days they can only view saved data until they pay for access.
saas/paid/cases/failed.question: The payment failed. What happens with a new account, and what with a customer who's already using it?
saas/paid/cases/failed.help: Separate the first purchase from a renewal. Write whether an existing customer gets extra days.
saas/paid/cases/failed.example: The new account is switched off. An existing customer has 7 days to fix their card, then the ability to add new things is closed.
saas/paid/cases/cancel.question: The customer has cancelled the renewal, but the paid period is still running. Until when do they use it?
saas/paid/cases/cancel.help: Write until when what they've already paid for keeps working, and that the next fee isn't charged.
saas/paid/cases/cancel.example: They use it until the end of the paid month. The next payment isn't taken.
saas/paid/cases/ended.question: The paid period has ended. Can they still view or download saved materials?
saas/paid/cases/ended.help: Ending access, deleting the account and deleting the materials are separate decisions.
saas/paid/cases/ended.example: They can view and download saved documents. They can't add new ones or change them.
hardware.title: Hardware
hardware.intro: Turn the initial estimates from Idea into numbers, suppliers, tests and a list of what still blocks the build.
hardware/spec.title: Formalize the requirements of the first version
hardware/spec.guide_body:
From estimate to specification
Preparation for a physical product is the move from knowing “is this feasible” to a document saying “exactly how we'll build it”. Idea answered the questions about feasibility, costs, time, demand and compliance — in the form of initial estimates. The task of this stage isn't to repeat the tests but to translate the results into a measurable specification that can be delivered without guesswork.
Every constraint from the earlier tests — durability, weight, energy use, accuracy — now gets a numerical value and a status: mandatory or desirable.
On this basis, list the key subassemblies, separate the critical parts from the auxiliary ones and assign each module to a category: must have, should have, could have, not now. Finally, check that the scope covers all mandatory requirements. If it doesn't, the gap has to be closed before anyone starts designing.
§
Measurable requirements
Turn loose ideas into numbers. Instead of writing that the device should be “light and run for a long time”, write down specific parameters: the maximum weight, the dimensions and the required battery life.
Precise numbers from day one limit misunderstandings between the product person and the person building it, and let you check progress.
§
Minimum and target
For each parameter, set two values: the absolute minimum threshold needed to launch a working first version, and the target value you'll aim for later.
Separating these values protects you from constantly adding improvements and lets you release a stable first version without postponing the start indefinitely.
§
Mandatory and desirable
Split the functions into critical and additional ones. Describe the expected effect, for example “the device sends data wirelessly every 5 seconds”, not a specific circuit solution, for example “we use module X”.
Collect this in one record available to the whole team. Otherwise it's easy to end up with two contradictory versions of the assumptions.
hardware/spec/numbers.title: Parameters that can be measured
hardware/spec/numbers/requirements.quest: Write down the functions and constraints as measurable requirements.
hardware/spec/numbers/requirements.help: One item is one parameter. The minimum has to be met in the first version. The target is left for later. Priority: mandatory or desirable.
hardware/spec/numbers/requirements.examp: Battery life. Minimum 8 hours, target 12 hours, mandatory. Weight. Minimum up to 300 g, target up to 250 g, desirable.
hardware/spec/numbers/requirements.confi: E.g. battery life on one charge
hardware/supply.title: Formalize suppliers and production
hardware/supply.guide_body:
Why suppliers weigh as much as the specification
Complete the initial quotes and supplier lists from Idea with hard data: minimum order quantities, availability, substitutes for critical parts, maximum lead time, the tools and machines required, and geographical, legal and trade restrictions.
This is where the risks that later delay production the most usually come out.
§
Prices, quantities and availability
Turn the initial list of parts into one file for the first batch. Collect unit prices, availability and minimum order quantities.
A common trap: the manufacturer requires buying thousands of units of a chip, while you're assembling a short batch. Checking these numbers early protects you from freezing cash in surplus parts.
§
Substitutes
Name the subassemblies most exposed to price swings or shortages and find a substitute or a second supplier for them.
The lack of one small chip can halt production for a long time. An approved substitute is a safeguard, not decoration on the list.
§
Delivery time and tools
Set the maximum waiting time for key parts and the machines, molds and test tools needed for production.
A dedicated injection mold for the enclosure can take 8–12 weeks. Put this date in the plan right away, so you don't stall the assembly of the batch.
§
Customs and transport
Include customs duty, import and export requirements and the real transport time in the calculation.
The cost per unit isn't just the distributor's price. Freight, taxes and customs handling change the final margin and the date.
hardware/supply/bom.title: Parts for the first batch
hardware/supply/bom/parts.question: Collect the prices, minimum order and availability of the parts.
hardware/supply/bom/parts.help: One item is one part or material. Enter an unknown price as “to be checked”, not as zero.
hardware/supply/bom/parts.example: Enclosure. $4.50 per unit with a minimum order of 200. Available, delivery 6 weeks.
hardware/supply/backup.title: Substitutes and tools
hardware/supply/backup/seconds.question: Which parts are risky and what substitute do they have?
hardware/supply/backup/seconds.help: Enter the parts whose shortage or price jump would halt the batch. If there are none, leave the list empty and save.
hardware/supply/backup/seconds.example: Microcontroller A. Substitute: chip B, already tested on a sample.
hardware/supply/backup/tools.question: What tools, machines or molds are needed for the first batch?
hardware/supply/backup/tools.help: For each item, add the approximate time needed to prepare it, if you know it.
hardware/supply/backup/tools.example:
Injection mold for the enclosure. Preparation about 10 weeks.
A station for leak testing.
hardware/supply/backup/logistics.questio: What customs duty, import and export rules and transport time go into the cost and the date?
hardware/supply/backup/logistics.help: If you sell and manufacture in one country and don't see such costs, say so directly.
hardware/supply/backup/logistics.example: Parts from Asia: freight and duty about 12% of the value. Transport 4 weeks. This goes into the unit price.
hardware/quality.title: Define quality, safety and reliability
hardware/quality.guide_body:
Quality before the product reaches the market
Translate the problems from the prototype tests into conditions whose fulfilment can be measured. Treat safety requirements as non-negotiable, regardless of time or budget pressure.
§
Safe use
Turn technological risks and usage scenarios into guidelines meant to prevent failure.
Define the conditions for safe operation in normal use and in foreseeable misuse: a drop, the wrong charger, moisture. Designing with user error in mind reduces later returns.
§
Durability and error threshold
Define the planned lifetime under real conditions and the acceptable rate of rejects in production and failures at customers.
No device is failure-free. A limit, for example below 1% failures per year, lets you plan replacements and inspection instead of assuming zero.
§
It can be checked
Phrase each requirement so that it can be checked by a measurement, a test or a procedure.
Instead of “the enclosure must be sturdy” write: “the enclosure survives a drop from 1.2 m onto concrete without cracking”.
hardware/quality/safe.title: Safe use and error threshold
hardware/quality/safe/use.question: How should the product behave in normal use and in a foreseeable user error?
hardware/quality/safe/use.help: A drop, the wrong power supply, moisture, a child nearby — only what really applies to this device.
hardware/quality/safe/use.example: When dropped from a desk, the enclosure doesn't crack. The wrong charger mustn't damage the battery or heat up the enclosure.
hardware/quality/safe/life.question: How long should it work, and what rate of faults or rejects do you accept?
hardware/quality/safe/life.help: Give a period and a number. “Few failures” can't be checked.
hardware/quality/safe/life.example: A year of daily use. Below 2% of units rejected at inspection and below 1% failures in the first year.
hardware/quality/tests.title: How you'll check it
hardware/quality/tests/checks.question: Write down the requirements so that they can be measured.
hardware/quality/tests/checks.help: One item is one test or measurement.
hardware/quality/tests/checks.example: Water resistance. Submersion for 30 minutes at a depth of 1 m, no water inside.
hardware/rules.title: Translate the regulations into product features
hardware/rules.guide_body:
Regulations as features, not slogans
Map the regulations and certificates from Idea onto specific product features, the documentation required, the scope of testing and the markings. Check whether a legal requirement clashes with a technical assumption while there's still time to change it.
§
What a regulation changes in the design
Link the requirements to specific solutions: choice of material, grounding, board layout.
Electromagnetic compatibility and electrical safety taken into account at the schematic stage limit costly fixes after failed tests.
§
Documents and tests
Make a list of the documents, reports and standards in the chosen markets, for example CE or FCC, and assign them to the stage at which they're needed.
Certification requires complete technical documentation. Collecting it as you go limits downtime right before sales.
§
Labels and instructions
Define the content, symbols and format of the rating plates, warning stickers and instructions required in the market you're starting in.
A missing required symbol, for example the crossed-out bin, can stop a delivery or make sales impossible.
§
Does the regulation clash with the rest
Check whether a legal requirement contradicts the dimensions, the weight or the way of use. Resolve it before building.
Example: a thicker insulating enclosure changes the dimensions while still on the drawing, before you order the molds.
hardware/rules.guide_sources.0: Y Combinator, Standard Startup Documents & Legal Resources (2023).
hardware/rules/map.title: Regulations and markings
hardware/rules/map/links.question: Which regulation or certificate changes a specific feature of the product?
hardware/rules/map/links.help: One item is one standard, mark or obligation. Add which part of the product it concerns.
hardware/rules/map/links.example: Electrical safety. An enclosure made of a material that doesn't sustain a flame. Testing before sales in the EU.
What it changes in the product
E.g. before the first sale in the EU
hardware/rules/map/labels.question: What has to be on the label and in the instructions in the market you're starting in?
hardware/rules/map/labels.help: Content, marks and language. If you don't know yet, write “to be checked” next to the specific mark, don't skip the market.
hardware/rules/map/labels.example: Product name, manufacturer details, the crossed-out bin symbol and a short warning in the local language.
hardware/rules/map/clash.question: Does any regulation clash with the earlier requirements? How are you resolving it?
hardware/rules/map/clash.help: If there's no contradiction, write “No contradiction” and, in one sentence, what was checked.
hardware/rules/map/clash.example: Insulation forces a thicker enclosure. We're raising the allowed dimension from 80 mm to 92 mm. The weight still stays within the minimum.
hardware/readiness.title: Settle the resources and open problems before building
hardware/readiness.guide_body:
An open list of what's still unresolved
The result of this stage isn't a finished product. The result is a specification, supplier data, quality and regulatory requirements and a list of open risks that lets you start building without guessing what's to be made.
For each open risk from Idea, judge whether you can start despite it or whether resolving it is a condition for starting. Not every problem has to stop the project. Each has to be deliberately postponed, not overlooked.
§
Who and what is missing
List the specialists, labs, contractors and machines needed for building. Mark what you already have and what has to be obtained.
Your own machine park or a full-time niche specialist usually isn't needed at this stage. An external lab or an engineer for a specific test is often faster.
§
Budget with a buffer
Set aside an amount for tools, prototypes, tests and consultations based on the earlier points.
Add a buffer of about 15–20% for a board revision or an extra lab session. In hardware, things rarely work out the first time.
§
What blocks the start of building
Write down the current technical, cost, production and regulatory risks.
Separate the ones that have to be resolved before building from those that can wait. Effort goes into the risk that can stop the project, not into a detail that can wait.
hardware/readiness/resources.title: People, tools and budget
hardware/readiness/resources/needs.quest: What do you need for building, and do you already have it?
hardware/readiness/resources/needs.help: A specialist, a lab, a manufacturer or a machine. If it's missing, write where you'll get it.
hardware/readiness/resources/needs.examp: A water-resistance lab. We don't have one. We'll rent one test before the mold.
hardware/readiness/resources/needs.confi: We have it or need to get it
We have it, we'll rent it, we're looking
hardware/readiness/resources/budget.ques: What budget are you setting aside for tools, prototypes, tests and consultations?
hardware/readiness/resources/budget.help: Base the amount on the previous points and add a buffer of about 15–20% for the fix that will come up on the first attempt.
hardware/readiness/resources/budget.exam: The mold, two board iterations and one test: $7,000 plus a 20% buffer, about $8,400 in total.
hardware/readiness/risks.title: What's still open
hardware/readiness/risks/open.question: Which technical, cost, production or regulatory risks are still open?
hardware/readiness/risks/open.help: For each one, write whether it blocks the start of building or can wait. If the list is empty, leave it and save — that means you don't see an open risk.
hardware/readiness/risks/open.example: The price of the radio chip is unknown. We need to know it before ordering the batch. The enclosure color can wait.
b2b.title: B2B
b2b.intro: Prepare the path from the first contact with a company to the day it can start using it.
b2b/sales.title: Prepare the sales process
b2b/sales.guide_body:
A short path, not a long procedure
Lay out the path from the first contact to the start of cooperation. Remove the steps that drag out the decision or confuse the other side. The simpler the path, the easier it is for a company to get to a purchase.
In selling to companies, three or four steps are usually enough: a conversation and understanding the need, a short demo of a tailored solution, an offer, closing.
§
What really moves a company forward
For each stage, write down the event after which the company can move on: a demo, the approval of the person with the budget, a request for an offer.
Don't move a deal forward just because the conversation was pleasant. Rely on a signal: a returned description of needs, the presence of the person who controls the budget.
§
A list of companies instead of a separate system
Keep track of the companies you're talking to or want to contact: the current stage, the next step and the person on your team.
At the start, this list is enough. You don't need a separate sales program. What matters is that the whole team sees the next step and when it's to happen.
b2b/sales/steps.title: The path from contact to cooperation
b2b/sales/steps/path.question: Put the stages in order and write what moves a company forward.
b2b/sales/steps/path.help: One item is one stage. Keep only the steps you really have.
b2b/sales/steps/path.example: Conversation. Next, when the other side describes a specific problem and agrees to a demo. Demo. Next, when they ask for an offer.
b2b/sales/steps/path.config.columns.forw: What has to happen to move on
A specific event, not “a good conversation”
b2b/sales/accounts.title: Companies you're talking to
b2b/sales/accounts/companies.question: Enter the companies you're already talking to or want to contact.
b2b/sales/accounts/companies.help: For each: the current stage, the next action and who on your team is responsible for it. If you're working alone, enter your name.
b2b/sales/accounts/companies.example: Studio Nord. After the first conversation. Send the offer on Thursday. Kuba.
b2b/offer.title: Prepare the first offer
b2b/offer.guide_body:
What exactly you're selling
Describe the scope of the first version in the language of benefits, not a list of technologies. Base it on what's to be built as the first version.
Keep a fixed core of the offer. Avoid designing everything from scratch for each customer.
§
Price and time
Give the price or the way it's calculated, what exactly the customer pays for and how long the cooperation or delivery lasts.
A free trial period rarely builds a company's commitment. If you need a trial, consider a paid pilot at a lower cost or a clear refund condition. A customer who puts down even a small amount takes the test more seriously.
§
A pilot has an end
If there's a test, define in advance what the customer gets and what makes you consider it finished. If there's no test, write “Not applicable”.
A pilot without a goal can drag on without a decision. Set one indicator, for example: “If the team saves 5 hours within 14 days, we move on to a contract”.
b2b/offer/scope.title: What you're selling and for how much
b2b/offer/scope/what.question: What scope of the first version can you offer a company?
b2b/offer/scope/what.help: Base it on what's to be built for the first version in General. Write what the customer gets, not how it's built.
b2b/offer/scope/what.example: A request form for the reception desk and a weekly summary of how many requests were closed.
b2b/offer/scope/price.question: What's the price or how do you calculate it, and what exactly does the customer pay for?
b2b/offer/scope/price.help: An amount, a rate or a formula. Add whether it's a subscription, a setup or both.
b2b/offer/scope/price.example: $600 for setup and $200 a month for use by up to 5 people.
b2b/offer/scope/term.question: How long does the cooperation or delivery last?
b2b/offer/scope/term.help: If time doesn't matter, write “No set end” and what ends the cooperation in that case.
b2b/offer/scope/term.example: Setup 3 weeks. The subscription is open-ended, with one month's notice.
b2b/offer/pilot.title: A test, if one is needed
b2b/offer/pilot/deal.question: What does the customer get in the test, and what makes you consider it finished?
b2b/offer/pilot/deal.help: If there's no test, write “Not applicable”.
b2b/offer/pilot/deal.example: 14 days with one team. It ends when we count the hours saved and the customer decides whether to take the subscription.
b2b/kickoff.title: Prepare the start of cooperation
b2b/kickoff.guide_body:
Scope, before you start building for the customer
Go back to the findings from the idea stage and list the features essential to the promised benefit. Only then define the account structure, roles, permissions and integrations, and what you're postponing for later.
On this basis you can close the scope of the first version and write what makes you consider a part done.
§
One company's data mustn't leak to another
Define how you separate the data of individual companies, what the scope of user access is and what integrations are needed.
Write down the technical constraints that affect building. Especially the situation in which a wrong access configuration would show one customer's data to another.
§
Security and paperwork
Define what business and personal data you'll process, who has access to it, how it's protected and when it should be deleted.
List the requirements typical of companies, for example single sign-on, and the documents: terms of service, a policy, a data processing agreement if you process personal data.
Make a checklist out of this and confirm it before you make the product available to a customer.
§
The team and the budget for starting delivery
Define the roles and skills, assign responsibility and point out the gaps: you do it yourselves, you outsource it or you look for a person.
Prepare the tools, the budget and the time frame. Check whether that's enough for the agreed scope. Before building, the team should know it has the skills, the means and the time, rather than discovering a gap along the way.
§
From purchase to first use
Describe the customer's path from purchase to use: what information, access and configuration are needed and who is responsible for them.
Work out how you handle requests and how you hand the customer over between sales, setup and support, so information doesn't get lost along the way.
§
What you need from the customer
List the materials, data, access and approvals the customer has to hand over before the start. If you don't need anything, say so directly.
The fewer tasks at the very beginning, the faster the customer gets to first use. A simple list for them is enough.
§
Division of work
List what your team does before the start and what the customer does. Assign people on both sides.
The most common delay is the lack of a lead person on the customer's side. Make sure one is named from day one.
§
Formalities along the way
Lay out the steps from the approval of the purchase to the moment the customer uses the solution on their own. Include the contract, an NDA, a purchase order or an invoice, if you have them.
A template and an electronic signature shorten the time from decision to the first real benefit. That's the goal of this point.
b2b/kickoff/needs.title: What has to happen before the start
b2b/kickoff/needs/from_client.question: What do you need from the customer before they start using it?
b2b/kickoff/needs/from_client.help: Data, access, approvals, materials. If you don't need anything, enter “Nothing”.
b2b/kickoff/needs/from_client.example:
A list of the people who will get access.
A person on the customer's side who takes questions.
b2b/kickoff/needs/ours.question: What does your team have to do before the start?
b2b/kickoff/needs/ours.example:
Set up the company's space.
Send the contract for signature.
b2b/kickoff/needs/theirs.question: What does the customer have to do before the start?
b2b/kickoff/needs/theirs.help: One action per item. If the list is only “Nothing”, enter that as one entry.
b2b/kickoff/needs/theirs.example:
Sign the contract.
Name the lead person on their side.
b2b/kickoff/start.title: From approval to first use
b2b/kickoff/start/path.question: What are the successive actions from confirming the purchase to the moment the customer can use it?
b2b/kickoff/start/path.help: Add the formalities you have: a contract, an NDA, a purchase order, an invoice, materials.
b2b/kickoff/start/path.example:
We sign the contract.
We issue the invoice for the setup.
We set up access and agree on the time of first use.
b2b/kickoff/start/data.question: What customer data will you have, and who outside this company can see it?
b2b/kickoff/start/data.help: Personal data, company data, files. If two customers mustn't see each other's materials, say so directly. When you don't process customer data, write “We don't process customer data”.
b2b/kickoff/start/data.example: We have employees' names and the content of the requests. Only this company and the person on our team running the setup can see them. Another customer can't see this.
b2c.title: B2C
b2c.intro: Work out how the buyer can cancel or report that the purchase doesn't work, and how you'll handle it in the first version.
b2c/returns.title: Prepare returns and complaints
b2c/returns.guide_body:
What returns depend on
The rules depend on the country you start selling in and on whether you sell online or in person. First write down the channel, the payment and the delivery. Without this, cancelling a purchase can't be described sensibly.
Write down when the customer can cancel and what you have to do if the purchase doesn't work as promised. If a deadline hasn't been checked yet, write “to be checked” next to the specific rule. Don't guess the number.
§
What the product does and what you do by hand
For a return and, separately, for a complaint, write down how the customer reports it.
On the side of the product or the point of sale, at the start it's enough to have what lets the customer find a contact and say which purchase the report concerns.
The rest you can do by hand: check the report, reply and arrange the refund. Agree on this split with the person building the first version.
b2c/returns.guide_sources.0: Withdrawal and complaint rules appropriate to the country and the way of the first sale.
b2c/returns/channel.title: What the first purchase looks like
b2c/returns/channel/where.question: Where does the first sale take place, and how does the buyer pay and receive the purchase?
b2c/returns/channel/where.help: Online or in person, the payment method and the delivery method. Returns depend on this.
b2c/returns/channel/where.example: An online shop. Payment with the order. A parcel by courier or personal pickup.
b2c/returns/rights.title: When the buyer can back out
b2c/returns/rights/rule.question: When can the customer cancel the purchase, and what do you have to do if the purchase doesn't work as promised?
b2c/returns/rights/rule.help: Take into account the country you're starting in and the way of selling. If a deadline hasn't been checked yet, write “to be checked” next to the specific rule, don't guess the number.
b2c/returns/rights/rule.example: Online sales in the EU: the customer can withdraw within 14 days of receipt. When the product doesn't work, we accept the complaint and refund the money or replace the item.
b2c/returns/handling.title: How you'll handle a return and a complaint
b2c/returns/handling/flow.question: For a return and for a complaint, write down how the customer will report it and what you'll do.
b2c/returns/handling/flow.help: A return and a complaint separately. Write what the product or the point of sale has to be able to do, and what you'll do by hand.
b2c/returns/handling/flow.example: Return. The customer writes to the address from the order confirmation and gives the number. We check the deadline, confirm receipt of the parcel and arrange the refund.
b2c/returns/handling/flow.config.columns: What the product or the sale has to allow
E.g. finding the contact and the purchase number
